content.text: Examining candidate sources for evaluating prediction error. Efron's work is promising, specifically "How Biased Is the Apparent Error Rate of a Prediction Rule?" (1986), which addresses the over-optimistic error estimation when using the same data for training and evaluation. Another Efron paper, "The Estimation of Prediction Error: Covariance Penalties and Cross-Validation" (2004) explores the connection between in-sample error and cross-validation techniques.

The literature review now highlights key papers that quantify the bias in in-sample error rates, and explain cross-validation approaches. Efron's work (1986, 2004) and Stone (1974) emphasize the need for out-of-sample assessment. Mallows (1973) introduced a bias penalty for assessing true prediction error. Gneiting (2011) and Willmott and Matsuura (2005) differentiate between MAE and MSE in assessing errors.

Examining literature focused on interpreting residual errors in model predictions. Chai and Draxler (2014) analyze how error metrics like RMSE and MAE impact residual interpretation based on underlying assumptions. Ye (1998) introduces generalized degrees of freedom for quantifying optimism in model selection. Berk et al. (2013) highlights the need for post-selection correction of statistical inference. Rosset and Tibshirani (2020) analyze training residual optimism. Varma and Simon (2006) focus on error estimation bias from cross-validation in model selection.

Focusing on forecast accuracy measures, the paper by Hyndman and Koehler (2006) offers a comprehensive evaluation of error metrics like MAE and MSE, statistically analyzing their properties, degeneration, and interpretation. The review has reached the target range of 10-15 papers, with 13 papers included. The paper count meets the specified criteria.
